title: Addressing fear
content:
_Don’t bring a spreadsheet to a fear fight._

Change causes fear. And change is all around us.

The fear of the unknown. The fear of failure. The fear of uncertainty.

Mostly, we’d like safety. And when the world changes, safety feels like it’s in short supply.

One reason we have security theatre is that the performance of security often creates more of the feeling we seek than actual safety.

Taking your shoes off before you enter the airport. Installing a giant, clunky, loud, armored garage door. Viewing strangers with suspicion. Using false proxies and useless shortcuts to insulate ourselves (or seek to do so) from the changes and the unknowns we fear.

Statistics rarely overcome stories.

So what does?

Familiarity. And conversation.

“What would make you feel safe?” is a different approach than “there’s nothing to be afraid of.”

_Until we get familiar enough with the new status quo, what performance would be a helpful way to create the feeling of safety?_

_What if we could create even more of that feeling with a different approach?_

_And while we’re at it, what if we spent time becoming familiar with the thing you’re afraid of?_

The most useful spreadsheets and facts are the ones that fearful people create to help them see their world differently.

title: New Feathered Dinosaur is the First Megaraptor Discovered in Europe
content:
England may have a reputation for bleak weather, but the Isle of Wight is closer to dreamy than dreary. The small, diamond-shaped island off the southern coast has sun-drenched beaches and microclimates warm enough for tropical plants. Of course, 120 million years ago, it was even toastier, featuring a lush sub-tropical landscape populated by dinosaurs. Now paleontologists have discovered a new Cretaceous creature that lived there, and it’s proving to be an important piece in the puzzle of megaraptor migration.

A team of paleontologists identified the new species from a partial braincase unearthed from the Isle of Wight in 1924 by an amateur paleontologist. The specimen was discovered after a century spent languishing in a drawer of England’s Natural History Museum. Once brought to light, the team performed micro-CT scans to create 3D models of the interior and exterior of the skull.

**Read more: “**[**This Newly Discovered Dinosaur Looks Terrifying—But Probably Wouldn’t Eat You**](https://nautil.us/this-newly-discovered-dinosaur-looks-terrifying-but-probably-wouldnt-eat-you-1285466)**”**

Comparisons to other dinosaur groups revealed it was a megaraptor—a family of bipedal predators with sharp claws that spread throughout the supercontinent of Gondwana during the Cretaceous. The opening of the skull where the spinal cord entered combined with a unique hour-glass-shaped crest indicated it was a previously unidentified species, and the team [published](http://dx.doi.org/10.1098/rsos.260937) their findings in the _Royal Society Open Science_.

The name they chose—_Invictibellatrix amberina_—carries a special meaning. The genus designation is Latin for “unconquered female warrior,” and it was given this sobriquet as a symbol of “hope and strength to all those who are bullied, discriminated, victimized and oppressed that tomorrow will be theirs and not to give up in the face of such odds.” (The species name, _amberina_, is a reference to fossilized amber found with the braincase.)

And it fits, too. Standing at around five feet tall and only 10-13 feet long, the dinosaur was far from an apex predator (unlike other megaraptors). Still, it definitely would have bullied us. “It was not the apex predator of its time, but for humans this dinosaur would have been more dangerous than a _T. rex_.” study author Cassius Morrison of the University College London said in a [statement](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/news/2026/oct/uk-dinosaur-fossil-identified-new-long-clawed-predator). “We would have been perfectly sized prey, about a third of their body weight. They definitely would have chased us. A _T. rex_ wouldn’t have bothered, as we would have been too small.”

While the braincase is all the paleontologists have to go on, they say the dinosaur likely had feathers, four- to eight-inch claws, and would have occupied a similar ecological niche as hyenas, feeding on smaller prey items like lizards, mammals, and other tiny dinos.

As the first megaraptor found in Europe, the discovery is also helping to fill in some gaps in the fossil record. Megaraptors are thought to have originated in what’s now Asia before migrating to other parts of Gondwana. Or as study Charlie Scherer of University College London explained, “This new species is the first proof we have that megaraptorans were also present in Europe and that they reached Gondwana this way rather than island-hopping further south.” ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

# ISS Astronaut Spots Moon-like Mountains From Space

Earth and the moon have a shared geological history

[DN](http://nautil.us/author/david-nield)

By [David Nield](http://nautil.us/author/david-nield)

3:00 PM CDT on October 14, 2026

[Add Nautilus to Google](https://google.com/preferences/source?q=nautil.us)

![Image 4](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/2026/10/ISS_header.jpeg?w=2880)

There may be a couple of hundred thousand miles between Earth and the moon, but our planet shares some striking geological similarities with our nearest neighbor in the sky. One of those similarities is the rock anorthosite.

[Video 2](http://nautil.us/iss-astronaut-spots-moon-like-mountains-from-space-1285807)

![Image 5](https://pl.primis.tech/live/liveView.php?&stnaInterval=0)![Image 6](https://pl.primis.tech/live/liveView.php?&stnaInterval=0)

The crystalline rock makes up much of the lunar highlands—it’s the lighter colored gray you can see when you look up at the moon—and its core mineral is the most common on the lunar surface. It’s thought to have formed during the initial cooling of the moon, as magma hardened into solid rock after [its violent birth](https://nautil.us/the-violent-birth-of-the-moon-505044).

On Earth, you can also find anorthosite across several continents, though it’s less widespread than it is on the moon. The photo below shows one of the larger collections of the rock on Earth, the Saririaky massif in Madagascar, estimated to be almost 40 square miles in area.

![Image 7](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/2026/10/01-massif.jpg?w=710)

The Saririaky anorthosite massif in southwestern Madagascar. _Credit: NASA_

[Subscribe to skip ads](http://nautil.us/products)Advertisement

This stunning image—revealing the pale anorthosite against the rock and soil around it—was snapped by an astronaut on board the International Space Station on August 28th. NASA [doesn’t say](https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/moon-like-madagascar/) which ISS crew member took the shot, though they note it was taken with a Nikon Z9 with a focal length of 400 millimeters.

The Saririaky massif is [the largest of four](https://doi.org/10.1007/s004100050461) anorthosite blocks in this part of southwestern Madagascar, with large-scale deformations of continental crust thought to be responsible for spreading the rock out to different regions. This particular massif is estimated to be at least 600 million years old, making it not quite as ancient as the 4-billion-year-old anorthosite on the moon.

![Image 8](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/2026/10/02-labels.jpg?w=710)

This is one of four similar massifs in southwestern Madagascar. _Credit: NASA_

While the composition of anorthosite can vary and doesn’t exactly match the mixtures on the moon, these outcrops on Earth are an invaluable way of studying what’s on the lunar surface without the need for any rockets, space suits, or moon buggies.

[Subscribe to skip ads](http://nautil.us/products)Advertisement

Scientists have previously identified anorthosite deposits in Montana [as being particularly moon-like](https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/montanas-moon-like-rocks-146650/), which means the rock can be used as a close analog for the lunar equivalent. These rocks are older as well, around 2.7 billion years in age. “These simulants are extremely helpful when it comes to testing equipment, space suits, or anything else that will come in contact with the lunar surface when humans go back to the moon,” NASA lunar geoscientist Sarah Deitrick explained in a [statement](https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/montanas-moon-like-rocks-146650/).

![Image 9](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/2026/10/03-montana.jpg?w=710)

Moon-like anorthosite has also been found in the Beartooth Mountains in Montana. _Credit: NASA Earth Observatory/Joshua Stevens_

To that end, NASA wants to get humans back on the moon in 2028, and lunar-like rocks here on Earth will be a crucial part of the preparation. ![Image 10](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

# This Prehistoric Alaskan Camp is Rewriting the History of Beringia

Stone tools point to a common culture

[JC](http://nautil.us/author/jake-currie)

By [Jake Currie](http://nautil.us/author/jake-currie)

1:01 PM CDT on October 14, 2026

[Add Nautilus to Google](https://google.com/preferences/source?q=nautil.us)

![Image 4](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-14-at-12.58.19-PM.png?w=2880)

When and how prehistoric humans came to the Americas has been the subject of some heated debate. For the latter half of the 20th century, it was thought that the Clovis people arrived first around 13,000 years ago. Beginning in the 1990s, the discovery of a slew of older sites—some as far south as Chile—seemed to upend that theory. Now a new study [published](http://dx.doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aeh0802) in _Science Advances_ is providing new fodder for debate—as well as some intriguing common threads between pre-Clovis and Clovis cultures.

[Video 2](http://nautil.us/this-prehistoric-alaskan-camp-is-rewriting-the-history-of-beringia-1285804)

![Image 5](https://pl.primis.tech/live/liveView.php?&stnaInterval=0)![Image 6](https://pl.primis.tech/live/liveView.php?&stnaInterval=0)![Image 7](https://pl.primis.tech/live/liveView.php?&stnaInterval=0)

A team of archeologists conducted a comprehensive survey of an ancient human settlement called Shég’ Xdaltth’í’ (pronounced shehg xuh-tuhl-TTH’EE) in Alaska Native Athabascan (which means “they were here”). The 13,800-year-old settlement is located on a windy bluff overlooking the Tanana River Valley in central Alaska, part of a vital corridor for prehistoric humans making their way through Beringia. The researchers conducted radiocarbon dating of the oldest sediment layer, analyzed the remains of plants and animals found there, and examined a staggering number of artifacts—more than 80,000 altogether.

**Read more:**[**“The Greatest Journey of All Time”**](https://nautil.us/the-greatest-journey-of-all-time-237889)

Far from being a brief stopover, the team says the site was a base camp, inhabited by prehistoric humans on and off for over two centuries. An oval dwelling with a hearth and an earthen oven showed evidence of cooking and discarded bones indicate they dined on mammoths, birds, hares, and other animals.

[Subscribe to skip ads](http://nautil.us/products)Advertisement

Some of these bones had been fashioned into fine tools like sewing needles and awls, which would have come in handy for stitching together animal hides to survive the harsh winters. They team also found an antler pendant, potentially decorative red ochre pigment, and the jawbone of a canid, which could indicate the ancient inhabitants were dog owners.

But most interesting were the stone tools, especially a collection of unique bipointed, diamond-shaped biface axes, which resemble those found both in western Beringia and northeastern arctic Siberia. According to the team the parallels point to a cultural connection that stretches across the Bering Strait.

And just as remarkable were the stone tools they _didn’t_ find: microblades. These stone-flake points with parallel sides were common in eastern Beringia sites around the same time, as well as other sites in Siberia. However, there doesn’t seem to be a connection between the microblades and the fluted points of paleoindian cultures much farther south. Instead, these cultures seem to use the same edge ground hafted biface technology discovered at Shég’ Xdaltth’í’.

The similarities between the cultures don’t stop there either. Paleoindians and the inhabitants of Shég’ Xdaltth’í’ both seemed to use red ochre as a decorative pigment, craft mammoth ivory into projectiles, and more. “The co-occurrence of these cultural features at the single site of Shég’ Xdaltth’í’ is truly notable,” the researchers write.

title: The Death of a Russian Plague Researcher, Explained by a Microbiologist
content:
Conflicting information about [the death of a lab worker](https://www.reuters.com/business/healthcare-pharmaceuticals/dozens-quarantined-siberia-after-plague-institute-lab-worker-dies-2026-10-05/) at a Russian plague research institute has fueled fears about the possibility of pneumonic plague spreading.

Nearly [200 people are in quarantine](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2026-101046) in Siberia after 28-year-old Darya Shipilova fell ill at work and [later died on October 2](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/05/russia-lab-worker-possibly-dies-of-plague-siberia-quarantine-measures-irkutsk).

The exact circumstances of her death are unknown. A senior Russian official [posted on social media](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-06/russia-pneumonia-death-sparks-speculation-of-plague-lab-leak/107231250) last week that Shipilova “had died from the plague”— before editing the post to add “possibly.” Russia’s [health watchdog](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/05/russia-lab-worker-possibly-dies-of-plague-siberia-quarantine-measures-irkutsk) has since stated she died from “pneumonia of unknown etiology.”

Local media reports [suggested](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/05/russia-lab-worker-possibly-dies-of-plague-siberia-quarantine-measures-irkutsk) she was infected following an accident at the lab where she worked, the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East. But these have not been confirmed.

So, what is plague, and how does it spread? Should we be worried?

**What Is Plague? Are There Different Types?**

Plague is [caused](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/plague) by the bacterium _Yersinia pestis_. The bacteria generally live in ground-dwelling rodents such as rats and prairie dogs, but can also infect humans.

The same _Y. pestis_ bacteria can cause three different types of plague.

Bubonic plague is spread from animals to humans by fleas, and causes swelling (called buboes) in the lymph nodes. Other [symptoms include](https://www.cdc.gov/plague/signs-symptoms/index.html) fever, headache, chills and weakness.

Bubonic plague can kill within a few days if antibiotics are not used. Between [30-60 percent of people](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/plague) who contract this form of plague will die.

Septicemic plague occurs if bubonic plague is left untreated, or it can occur directly if the disease enters the bloodstream. Septicemic plague causes bleeding into the organs; the name refers to the serious blood infection, septicemia, that this form of the disease can cause.

Pneumonic plague—the suspected but unconfirmed cause of Shipilova’s death in Siberia—can occur when bubonic plague spreads to the lungs. But pneumonic plague can also spread from person to person via tiny respiratory droplets.

Pneumonic plague is the rarest but most [severe form](https://doi.org/10.1093/pastj/gtj001). The fatality rate is [up to 100 percent](https://theconversation.com/a-person-in-the-us-has-died-from-pneumonic-plague-its-not-just-a-disease-of-history-261088) if left untreated.

In addition to the other symptoms, pneumonic plague also includes severe [pneumonia](https://www.healthdirect.gov.au/pneumonia)—an infection of the lungs, in this case caused by bacteria.

**Isn’t Plague a Medieval Sickness?**

Bubonic plague was responsible for the death of tens of millions of people in the western Mediterranean between 541-750CE (the [Plague of Justinian](https://origins.osu.edu/connecting-history/covid-justinianic-plague-lessons)) and [killed](https://origins.osu.edu/connecting-history/covid-black-death-plague-lessons) up to half of Europe’s population in the middle ages (the Black Death).

But there have been outbreaks since medieval times.

A [third pandemic](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspb.2018.2429) spanning the end of the nineteenth century and beginning of the twentieth [killed up to 12 million people](https://www.crassh.cam.ac.uk/research/projects-centres/visual-representations-of-the-third-plague-pandemic/).

Plague is [still endemic](https://www.cdc.gov/plague/maps-statistics/index.html) to Central Asia, Africa, the Americas and [Siberia](https://www.reuters.com/business/healthcare-pharmaceuticals/dozens-quarantined-siberia-after-plague-institute-lab-worker-dies-2026-10-05/), where the Russian lab worker died last week. This means it is present at a steady, consistent level in these regions.

Cases typically occur in [rural and agricultural areas](https://theconversation.com/a-person-in-the-us-has-died-from-pneumonic-plague-its-not-just-a-disease-of-history-261088) which makes a potential lab leak in an urban area unusual.

**Can It Be Treated?**

Yes. A 10-14-day course of antibiotics (either oral or intravenous) [treats the plague](https://www.cdc.gov/plague/hcp/clinical-care/index.html)—as long as they are taken soon after infection.

However, since 1995, several antibiotic-resistant strains have been [detected in the wild](https://doi.org/10.24171/j.phrp.2021.0288).

In the 1980s, Soviet Union scientists also engineered [resistant strains](https://www.popularmechanics.com/science/a74033610/russia-plague-lab-worker-dies/)—this history forms the basis of [hypothetical scenarios](https://theconversation.com/the-threat-of-biological-warfare-is-real-a-new-book-describes-the-potential-devastation-288934) involving biological warfare.

However, there is no evidence the strain alleged to have killed Shipilova could not be treated by antibiotics or that the lab is researching biological weapons.

**How Worried Should We Be?**

There has only been one documented major outbreak of the [pneumonic plague](https://academic.oup.com/past/article-abstract/190/1/147/1450013), in the 1910s in China.

We still don’t know much about the case in Siberia. But at this stage, there’s little evidence to cause concern about potential for an epidemic (which is localised) or a pandemic (which involves multiple countries).

In a [statement on Monday](https://www.newsweek.com/russias-response-to-suspected-plague-outbreak-under-scrutiny-12523852), the World Health Organization (WHO) said it was aware of reports a laboratory worker in Irkutsk had “died of severe pneumonia” but no cause of death had been officially confirmed.

The WHO statement also said: “Based on unofficial information available, the public health risk to the general population appears to be low. The risk assessment will be updated once more information is available.”

To assess this risk, access to transparent information about how Shipilova fell ill and died will be essential. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)![Image 2](https://assets.nautil.us/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: AI Safety Is Not A Corporate Plot
content:
AI companies like Anthropic and OpenAI have long mentioned the possibility that their products could be existentially dangerous, but this has recently crescendoed into even more dire warnings, including suggestions that we have to [pace the frontier](https://darioamodei.com/post/we-must-pace-the-frontier), ie coordinate to slow AI progress.

In response, cynical commentators have suggested this is a conspiracy to boost the companies’ stocks. The exact motives imputed vary from person to person. Some say the companies are hyping the product by talking about how dangerous it is; if AI is smart enough to kill all humans, it must be smart enough for your business workflow. Others say they’re trying to distract from near-term harms; every inch of newspaper space devoted to human extinction is one less inch that can be spent on plagiarism and water use. But the most popular story involves regulatory capture: if the product is unsafe, maybe it can only be trusted to a few big politically-connected companies, and everyone else should be banned.

Many debates about AI are complicated and hard to resolve, but this one isn’t: all of these stories are clearly false. Some evidence:

*   The AI experts who aren’t affiliated with big companies are just as concerned as the ones who are.

*   The AI company leaders giving these warnings were giving the exact same warnings before they had AI companies - and in many cases, before they worked in the industry, or before the industry existed.

*   If these corporate plots were real, they would be incredibly dumb.

Taking these in order:

[Grace et al](https://aiimpacts.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/ESPAI2024.pdf) surveyed 1,580 AI researchers who presented papers at big AI-related conferences, mostly academics with no company affiliation. Over half thought there was at least a 10% chance AI would cause “human extinction or similarly permanent and severe disempowerment of the human species”. 72% said we needed to be prioritizing AI safety research more. This survey was in 2024; current numbers would probably be higher.

Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio, and Yann LeCunn are collectively considered “the godfathers of AI” for inventing deep learning; in 2018, they received the Turing Award, sometimes called the Nobel Prize of computer science, for their accomplishment. In 2023, Geoffrey Hinton [quit his job](https://mitsloan.mit.edu/ideas-made-to-matter/why-neural-net-pioneer-geoffrey-hinton-sounding-alarm-ai) at Google to work full-time raising awareness of the potential existential dangers of AI; he said there was “between 10% and 50% chance” that his invention would destroy humanity. In the same year, Yoshua Bengio _also_[switched to activism](https://yoshuabengio.org/en/blog/professor-yoshua-bengios-speech-un-security-council), saying that he “regretted his life’s work” and that AI could have a “catastrophic impact”. Neither was affiliated with a major AI company.

(the third godfather, Yann LeCunn, runs a $3 billion AI company, and says he isn’t worried)

Along with these independent researchers, there are many others who formerly worked at companies, then quit to whistleblow about the dangers, or left to pursue anti-AI activism full-time. [Paul Christiano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Christiano) left OpenAI in 2021 to found an AI alignment nonprofit; he later said there was a “50/50 chance of doom shortly after you have AI systems that are human level.” [Daniel Kokotajlo](https://time.com/collections/time100-ai-2024/7012881/daniel-kokotajlo/) quit OpenAI in 2024, refusing to sign a non-disparagement clause even though it could have cost him $2 million in equity, in order to start a nonprofit warning about risks from AI (he says he thinks there’s about an 80% chance AI kills everyone). [Jacob Coxon](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/as-ai-behavior-raises-concerns-ex-researcher-jacob-coxon-warns-what-may-lie-ahead) quit Anthropic in September, also likely giving up millions of dollars in equity, because he thought it was “gambling with our lives”. There are dozens of others.

The people at AI companies are no more likely to raise the alarm about AI dangers than people who were never at AI companies, or people who were previously at AI companies but have since quit.

**DARIO AMODEI**first started discussing the risk of superintelligence destroying humanity in 2013, before OpenAI or Anthropic was founded, and when Amodei wasn’t employed in tech at all. [Here’s a 62 page debate](https://intelligence.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/01/10-27-2013-conversation-about-MIRI-strategy.pdf)between Amodei, Eliezer Yudkowsky, and other AI safety enthusiasts about strategy, dated October 27, 2013:

[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!2uht!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fcf3996a1-6e32-47fb-9120-8713b3e90565_741x719.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!2uht!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fcf3996a1-6e32-47fb-9120-8713b3e90565_741x719.png)

In 2017, when Amodei was an ordinary employee at OpenAI, he spoke about his work [the on the podcast 80,000 Hours](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/the-world-needs-ai-researchers-heres-how-to-become-one/) (July 21, 2017):

> I mainly work on safety. We have a safety team that’s so far, myself and Paul Christiano. Paul was co-author of mine on the [[Concrete Problems In AI Safety]](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.06565) paper and has also written a lot online on his blog about AI. He’s probably one of the people who’s I think done the most to promote clear thinking about the problem and tie it to current AI. We have a third person joining in a few weeks who I’m super excited about. We’re trying to build up a team that focuses on technical safety. We also do a little bit of strategy stuff which is how do we get different organizations that are working on AI to cooperate with each other, how do we cooperate with policy makers on questions like these. We’re also thinking a little bit about those issues but mainly technical safety.

Dario expanded on the cooperation point - he told the host about his fear that AI would lead to an “arms race” in which companies competed to develop the technology first and let safety slide. His solution was making companies cooperate:

> We all think about AGI and think, that safety issues are important. . . then the question is, how does that scale to there being a lot of organizations? How does that scale to others who get involved once they see how powerful AI is? Can we make them cooperate as well? My hope is that we can.

This became an obsession with him, and he hired an advisor to help OpenAI work on the problem. According to [the New Yorker](https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2026/04/13/sam-altman-may-control-our-future-can-he-be-trusted):

> In 2017, Amodei hired Page Hedley, a former public-interest lawyer, to be OpenAI’s policy and ethics adviser. In an early PowerPoint presentation to executives, Hedley outlined **how OpenAI might avert a “catastrophic” arms race—perhaps by building a coalition of A.I. labs that would eventually coördinate with an international body** akin to _NATO_, to insure that the technology was deployed safely.
> 
> 
> As Hedley recalled it, [OpenAI president Greg] Brockman didn’t understand how this would help the company beat its competitors. “No matter what I said,” Hedley told us, “Greg kept going back to ‘So how do we raise more money? How do we win?’

This incident and several like it turned Dario against Greg, leading to an era of constant backstabbing office politics. Dario led a pro-safety faction against Greg’s pro-business faction; Greg usually won. It didn’t help that Dario was anxious to the point of paranoia, constantly insisting that their work was too dangerous to release:

![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!mU0u!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3b046705-8904-4b4f-9e43-b758a6e2c8c1_952x362.png)

Sam Altman tried to play peacemaker by promising Dario various concessions, but eventually Dario noticed that Altman lied constantly and never came through on any of them, so he and the rest of the safety faction left to found Anthropic. [Here’s how Fortune described the split](https://fortune.com/2026/02/19/openai-anthropic-sam-altman-dario-amodei-refused-to-hold-hands-ai-super-bowl-ad-war-ceos-big-tech-conflict/):

> Amodei, along with a small group of employees, became concerned about OpenAI’s direction and what he perceived as a lack of safety involved in scaling up ChatGPT.
> 
> 
> In 2021, Amodei, along with his sister and cofounder Daniela Amodei and a dozen other ex-OpenAI employees started Anthropic with a mission to put safety first. The company released its large language model, Claude, in 2023.
> 
> 
> The employees who jumped ship from OpenAI believed two things, Amodei told _Fortune_’s Jeremy Kahn at the _Fortune Brainstorm Tech_ conference in 2023. First, they believed if you pour more compute into large language models, they will greatly improve, and there’s almost no limit to how advanced they can get. Second, they believed—in addition to scaling up the models—there needed to be a strong set of guardrails and safety considerations.

**SAM ALTMAN**[said](https://blog.samaltman.com/machine-intelligence-part-1)in February 2015 - that is, ten months before he started OpenAI - that “development of superhuman machine intelligence is probably the greatest threat to the continued existence of humanity.” He [continued](https://blog.samaltman.com/machine-intelligence-part-2):

> The US government, and all other governments, should regulate the development of SMI [superhuman machine intelligence]. In an ideal world, regulation would slow down the bad guys and speed up the good guys—it seems like what happens with the first SMI to be developed will be very important.
> 
> 
> Although my general belief is that technology is often over-regulated, I think some regulation is a good thing, and I’d hate to live in a world with no regulation at all. And I think it’s definitely a good thing when the survival of humanity is in question. (Incidentally, there is precedent for classification of privately-developed knowledge when it carries mass risk to human life. SILEX is perhaps the best-known example.)

He also famously said in June of that year that “AI will most likely lead to the end of the world, but in the meantime there will be great companies”. Some people say this was a “joke”. I think it was the one time in his life that Sam Altman was ever completely 100% honest.

**ELON MUSK,**another AI company leader who has been talking about extinction risk, has an equally long relationship with the topic. His [first statement](https://www.cnet.com/science/elon-musk-we-are-summoning-the-demon-with-artificial-intelligence/) on AI safety was in 2014, before he had any business ventures in AI, when he said that “We are summoning the demon with artificial intelligence”. He continued by calling it “our biggest existential threat”, and admitted that “I’m increasingly inclined to think **there should be some regulatory oversight, maybe at the national and international level** just to make sure that we don’t do something very foolish”.

Here’s a photo from [the first big AI Safety conference](https://futureoflife.org/event/ai-safety-conference-in-puerto-rico/) in Puerto Rico. Elon is circled in orange. He was a rare famous billionaire who agreed to hang out with powerless nerds to debate the safety of a technology that technically didn’t exist yet, just for the love of the game.

[![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!6WUN!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd0cd842e-337d-4773-936d-172dbc8eac8e_897x430.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!6WUN!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd0cd842e-337d-4773-936d-172dbc8eac8e_897x430.png)

The green circle is Demis Hassabis, the purple is Ilya Sutskever, and the red is Eliezer Yudkowsky.

After the conference, Elon [agreed to donate $10 million](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2015/jan/16/elon-musk-donates-10m-to-artificial-intelligence-research) to the fledgling cause. He continued to be a regular at AI safety conferences over the next few years. I saw him speak at the Asilomar conference in 2017, where he gave a rambling talk on how brain-computer interfaces could solve the problem (they didn’t).

**SHANE LEGG**and **DEMIS HASSABIS**are two of the three co-founders of DeepMind, now Google DeepMind. In 2008 - a year before founding Deep Mind - Legg wrote his PhD thesis on [“Machine Super Intelligence”](https://www.vetta.org/documents/Machine_Super_Intelligence.pdf), where he wrote that it could be “a nightmare scenario” (although he also said that “if we carefully prepare for this possibility in advance, not only might we avert disaster, we might bring about an age of prosperity unlike anything seen before.”) His other optimistic predictions [include](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/No5JpRCHzBrWA4jmS/q-and-a-with-shane-legg-on-risks-from-ai) “If by suffering you mean prolonged suffering, then I think this is quite unlikely. If a super intelligent machine (or any kind of super intelligent agent) decided to get rid of us, I think it would do so pretty efficiently.”

Hassabis was also concerned at least as early as 2012, when he reportedly [tried to convince Elon Musk](https://time.com/6310076/elon-musk-ai-walter-isaacson-biography/) that AI was an existential risk. He attended the same 2015 AI safety conference as Musk (see photo above) and [included as a condition](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2017/jan/26/google-deepmind-ai-ethics-board) of DeepMind’s acquisition by Google that Google set up a powerful AI safety oversight board (this went wrong in approximately every way possible).

**THE CORPORATE PLOT** hypothesis requires these CEOs to be the most prescient people in history. In 2008 or 2013 or 2015, when they were all in other industries and AI was just an academic curiosity, they would have had to realize that one day AI would become a trillion dollar business, that they would be the CEO of one of the companies, and that the company would benefit from regulatory capture. Then they would have had to devote a significant proportion of their life, and in some cases donate millions of dollars, to start laying the groundwork ahead of time, just in case it became necessary. Dario Amodei, while finishing his biology postdoc, would have to have moonlighted as an AI safety enthusiast just in case he became a multi-billion dollar tech CEO one day. Shane Legg would have had to choose his PhD thesis topic based on the possibility that he would own shares in a Google AI subsidiary sixteen years later.

The alternative is that all these people believed it then, and still believe it now, for the same reason that all of the independent experts and academics believe it. They are working in the field partly because they think that being closer to the development of AI gives them more of a chance to control it and keep it safe than if they were sitting on the sidelines.

Having shown that these men would have to be the smartest people in the world to pull this off, it’s worth noting that the plot they apparently dedicated their lives to is really dumb.

For example, if the Pacing The Frontier consortium attempt was a plot to pump stock prices, you might expect that, upon it being announced, stock prices would go up. [This didn’t happen](https://en.coinotag.com/openai-perp-sinks-13-percent-hyperliquid-anthropic-slowdown).

[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!GP_e!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fddc43691-5d75-4fc6-8e86-18a3ca5e5e3d_979x647.png)](https://en.coinotag.com/openai-perp-sinks-13-percent-hyperliquid-anthropic-slowdown?_x=1790147074954https://en.coinotag.com/openai-perp-sinks-13-percent-hyperliquid-anthropic-slowdown?_x=1790147074954)

Anthropic and OpenAI aren’t publicly traded companies, so they don’t have an easily-tracked stock price. But there are complicated cryptocurrency bets called “perpetual futures” that traders use to approximate the stock prices of private companies (usually these are some kind of prediction-market like instrument on eventual IPO price). When the slowdown call happened, Anthropic’s value on the biggest cryptocurrency futures platform dropped 4.57%, and OpenAI’s stock dropped 13.42%.

(two other AI companies that endorsed the slowdown proposal, Google DeepMind and X.AI, are subsidiaries of larger publicly traded companies; Google and SpaceX respectively. Both companies went down modestly the day after the announcement, although they have so many other things going on that I take this less seriously than the AI company futures.)

Why wouldn’t the stock market (or at least this particular cryptocurrency simulation of the stock market) approve of the slowdown as a potential regulatory moat? It seems like traders thought the first-level effects (slowing down) were more important than any secondary regulatory effects that might or might not materialize.

Libertarian economist Alex Tabarrok is head of the Center for Study of Public Choice, the subfield of economics that studies things like regulatory capture. He agrees with the traders. He wrote a good post, [What Regulatory Capture Actually Looks Like](https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/09/what-regulatory-capture-actually-looks-like.html), arguing that a regulatory capture story doesn’t fit:

> Go ahead: argue that Amodei and other AI experts are wrong about AI risk. Ask whether his proposals favor Anthropic. But calling “our product might kill you” a clever marketing and regulatory-capture strategy isn’t sophisticated analysis. The facts don’t fit regulatory capture theory and trying to make them fit requires epistemically painful Ptolemaic epicycles. Even a dull Ockham’s razor cuts through that story to the obvious alternative: Amodei actually believes what he’s saying.

Or consider another story - trying to distract from near-term harms. Is this really how things work? Are there vicious fights between environmentalists who want to save the rainforest and environmentalists who want to fight climate change, with the former arguing that the latter’s focus on longer-term risks detracts from environmental problems that are happening right now? No, obviously this is stupid; these groups are natural allies. Both donate to the Sierra Club and vote for the Green Party. Even if a certain rainforest supporter didn’t care about climate change at all, they would be grateful for the climate change activist’s votes and donations.

This is how things are shaping up with AI also. Last summer, Ted Cruz sponsored a bill to ban states from regulating AI. It had strong support from AI money and was expected to pass. A [coalition](https://encodeai.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/Coalition-Letter_-Oppose-the-Updated-AI-Moratorium.pdf) of effective altruist groups worried about human extinction, artists’ groups worried about intellectual property, family groups worried about harms to children, and many others united to defeat it.

But maybe it’s true for newspaper space in particular? Maybe concerns about human extinction are preventing journalists from writing about nearer-term harms?

Both people interested in human extinction and people interested in near-term harms fund the [Tarbell Center for AI Journalism](https://www.tarbellcenter.org/), which helps fund reporters on both category of risk (Tarbell received an ACX Grant two years ago). They highlight articles they’ve helped with on issues across the spectrum, from [Worried Anthropic Researchers Warn That AI Could Kill All Humans](https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/991927/anthropic-ai-kill-all-humans) to [Hundreds Gather To Urge Scottish Government To Pause Data Center Boom](https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026/sep/03/hundreds-holyrood-pause-scotland-datacentre-boom-ai) to [AI Is More Likely Than Humans To Form Biases When Hiring](https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/07/20/1140655/ai-biases-hiring-humans/).

In retrospect, this alliance should be obvious. Both groups want the same thing: the ability to slow AI. And both have the same enemy: the tsunami of Silicon Valley money which is trying to elect Congressmen who refuse to regulate AI in any way. Both groups are working together against their common foe. Signal-boosting long-term risks to distract from short-term risks would only empower this coalition, and so - like the other version of this plot - be implausibly stupid.

As for the claim that AI companies are trying to hype their products, this seems unnecessary: AI is the fastest-adopted technology in history:

[![Image 5: AI is the most rapidly adopted technology in history](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!yVUT!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F76e23b5c-2dc6-4942-9fdb-adce23b64ef6_619x443.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!yVUT!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F76e23b5c-2dc6-4942-9fdb-adce23b64ef6_619x443.png)

…so it hardly seems worth it to hype it up a little more at the cost of getting [a large number of Americans](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/16/poll-ai-technology-risks-humanity-trump-voters-01078087) to think your product will kill them personally, and a plurality of voters in both parties to want to ban your industry from creating new products:

[![Image 6](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!XudH!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F66ddfc96-408d-4181-a942-8be13be674bf_830x769.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!XudH!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F66ddfc96-408d-4181-a942-8be13be674bf_830x769.png)

If the last section required AI company leaders to be the smartest people in the world, this one requires them to be the dumbest.

We live in an age of cynicism and nihilism. When someone endorses a good cause, we accuse them of virtue-signaling; if they donate to it, we accuse them of trying to whitewash their role in capitalism. We lionize corrupt politicians and insipid bling-wielding celebrities because, as people who have never made any claim to moral acceptability, they are the only people who can entirely escape the suspicion of faking it.

This is idiotic and requires otherwise smart people to constantly contort themselves to figure out the latest less-than-entirely-depraved person’s angle. Maybe some people are so venal that they can’t imagine anyone truly caring about the welfare of humanity, but they should stop projecting this on everyone else. The experts are warning you that AI could kill you because they think AI could kill you. Many of them have made personal sacrifices to get the message out. Stop adding thumbtacks to your conspiracy corkboard and take their message seriously.

title: How Do Fungi Keep the Planet Healthy?
content:
People may think of soil as just dirt, but it is anything but inert. Beneath your feet, a vast network of mycorrhizal fungi is hard at work, trading minerals with plant roots. This trading system helps enrich the soil, and it sequesters 13 billion tons of atmospheric carbon dioxide each year — roughly equivalent to one-third of the world’s fossil-fuel emissions. Scientists know that these fungi form partnerships with 80% of all plant species on Earth, a relationship that evolved some 450 million years ago. What they have not understood is how organisms with no brain or central nervous system can decide whom to trade with, and on what terms.

Toby Kiers, an evolutionary biologist at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, has spent much of her career making this hidden world visible. Drawing on economics and game theory, and using tools that range from fluorescent quantum dots to imaging robots, her lab is probing how fungi and plants conduct their trade. The work raises new questions about soil, carbon, and even what counts as an individual organism. In this episode, Kiers tells co-host Steven Strogatz how these brainless, decentralized organisms can behave strategically — discriminating between better and worse partners and shifting resources across the network to wherever a plant will “pay” more for it — and how she has built a worldwide community of researchers to map the biodiversity of these underground networks and advocate for their protection.

Listen on [Apple Podcasts (opens a new tab)](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/the-joy-of-why/id1608948873), [Spotify (opens a new tab)](https://open.spotify.com/show/2FoxHraQSKwxV2HgUfwLMp), [TuneIn (opens a new tab)](https://tunein.com/podcasts/Science-Podcasts/The-Joy-of-Why-p1653040/) or your favorite podcasting app, or you can [stream it from Quanta](https://www.quantamagazine.org/tag/the-joy-of-why).

## **Transcript**

[_Music plays_]

**STEVE STROGATZ:**I’m Steve Strogatz.

**JANNA LEVIN:**And I’m Janna Levin.

**STROGATZ:**And this is _The Joy of Why._

**LEVIN:**A podcast from _Quanta Magazine_ where we explore some of the biggest unanswered questions in math and science today.

**STROGATZ:**Hey there, Janna. I would love to talk to you about a big question.

**LEVIN:**Okay.

**STROGATZ:**Imagine you’re walking around in the forest or in Central Park.

**LEVIN:**That’s my forest!

**STROGATZ:**I know, so what’s under your feet? What are your shoes hitting?

**LEVIN:**I think people would be very surprised that there’s real nature in Central Park. So you got the grass, you got the trees. Uh, there’s dirt. We have birds.

**STROGATZ:**Let’s focus on the dirt.

**LEVIN:**Is dirt our topic today?

**STROGATZ:**Dirt is related to our topic. We wanna talk about what’s happening underground in the form of what are called mycorrhizal fungi. I learned that I’m supposed to say fun-gee.

**LEVIN:**Not fun-guy?

**STROGATZ:**Not fun-guy.

**LEVIN:**I say fun- fung- fun-guy.

**STROGATZ:**Well, what would I say? I would probably s- I don’t know. Fun-ji?

**LEVIN:**So now I have to say fun-gee?

**STROGATZ:**You’re supposed to say fun-gee for the purpose of this episode.

**LEVIN:**Is that like saying Uranus?

**STROGATZ:**[_Laughs_] You should be saying that.

**LEVIN:**I do yeah.

**STROGATZ:**Well, so I spoke to someone recently that changed my perspective about these fungi under our feet and the wood wide web. Not the worldwide web, the wood wide web. It’s the mycorrhizal network of these vast networks of fungi that we never notice that are underground, and they’re incredibly important in connecting the roots and supplying nutrients to trees and other plants. Something like 80% to 90% of all the plant species all over the world are getting help from these fungi.

They’re also helping our atmosphere and our climate. They enrich the soil to help farmers and biodiversity, agriculture. They may even contribute to cloud formation through the release of their spores over rainforests.

**LEVIN:**Wow.

**STROGATZ:**So they may not get much respect, the fungi, but they’re right up there with the animals and plants in mattering to the world.

**LEVIN:**Yeah, ’cause you always hear about the role of bacteria, and so it’s really interesting how fungi could affect the whole ecosystem like that.

**STROGATZ:**Well, the bacteria are very intimately associated with these fungi. and That’s something that we’re going to hear from our guest about.

**LEVIN:**Alright.

**STROGATZ:**Toby Kiers is her name. She is an evolutionary biologist at the Vrije University in Amsterdam, and a recent MacArthur Fellow. So if you’re ready, here we go.

[_Music plays_]

**STROGATZ:**Welcome to _The Joy of Why_, Toby.

**TOBY KIERS:**Thanks so much about having me.

**STROGATZ:**Well, this is an area that is not familiar to me at all, and I’m dying to hear about it. Can you describe what your subject area is first, just in very broad terms?

**KIERS:**I study the class of organisms called mycorrhizal fungi, and the word mycorrhizal means _myco_, which means fungus, and _rhizal_, which means root. So these are a class of fungi that form a very intimate association with the vast majority of plants. So over 80% of all plant species on Earth form these partnerships, and it’s a very old partnership.

It evolved some 450 million years ago, and was actually really fundamental for plants that were in a wet, aquatic environment to start colonizing land hundreds of millions of years ago. And since then, it’s been an incredibly important relationship in building ecosystems that we live and survive on today.

And I don’t think many people know, but actually the fungus served as a plant root system for even tens of millions of years. Roots are kind of a new evolutionary innovation, so it’s a very intimate and old partnership between plants and fungi.

**STROGATZ:**So you’re saying the plants didn’t go to the bother of making their own roots? They were somehow using the fungi to do that for them?

**KIERS:**Exactly. So, what the plants were doing was they were sending carbon that they were photosynthesizing and taking out of the atmosphere and feeding it to these loose associations, these fungal networks that were in the soil, and in return they were getting resources like phosphorus and nitrogen. See, the thing that fungi are very good at is breaking up rocks and digesting these hard-to-access minerals.

And so they were feeding it to the plants, and in return the plants were giving carbon. And now this partnership really underlies our ecosystems on Earth.

**STROGATZ:**Oh, wow. I have all kinds of questions. First of all, very dramatic to say breaking up rocks. I don’t, just haven’t thought about it. What are they doing to break up rocks?

**KIERS:**Well, the fungi make these beautiful complex networks, and fungi are very good at digesting outside of their bodies and actually partnering with other microbes like bacteria that can help break down rocks. So, some people even say they’re very good at eating rocks on the outside of their bodies and having it dissolve into a form that can then be taken up.

And so the fungi then take up these nutrients and move them through these vast networks and feed them to plant roots. And in return —obviously they don’t do this for free — the plants are feeding them a diet of sugar and lipids like fats. It’s like the most brilliant diet of sugar and fats that is provided by the plants to the fungi. And this partnership is very common. It’s almost ubiquitous, I would say, across terrestrial ecosystems. And because of this partnership and because plants are constantly feeding carbon down to these networks, we actually call it one of Earth’s circulatory systems.

**STROGATZ:**Oh, nice. So, network is a word that everybody is using these days. We hear about the internet. We know we have our own circulatory system in our body, networks of blood vessels. But so when you talk about a mycorrhizal fungal network, what should I picture?

**KIERS:**Exactly. And it’s very clear. One thing I really want people to understand is that plants are not fungi , and fungi are not plants, and they’re very different kingdoms of life. So when you have a plant root and you were to pull it up from the ground, that’s a beautiful image, you would not quite be able to see these threads that are hanging from the root. They’re thinner than the hairs on my head, just a few microns across.

And the type that we really concentrate on are called arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, and we can get into where that name comes from. But these particular networks are like an open-pipe system. They’re literally like a tube. And in some senses, people think they’re the largest cells on Earth because they don’t have the septa that break it up into individual compartments.

And so a lot of what we do in the lab is growing these networks across sort of a transparent soil almost, like a way that you can see the networks and use microscopy to follow these networks and understand how they navigate space. We have developed together with biophysicists at the Biophysics Institute called AMOLF here in Amsterdam, these imaging robots that allow us to track individual nodes across these networks. So in any given experiment, we’re tracking about half a million of these nodes, these fungal decisions whether to go left or right or make a bridge when they fuse together.

And they actually make a beautiful supply chain because what you’re imagining —and I want you to really close your eyes and picture this — is that the plant is pouring carbon down into this root system, and the carbon, which now we can label with a fluorescent label, so we can actually watch it travel through this open-pipe system all the way down to the tips where the fungi use the carbon to keep building their network. Now, as they’re building that network, they’re collecting the phosphorus and the nitrogen in the water that they’re moving in an opposite direction back to the root system. Now, one of the most fascinating things about this symbiosis is that this is an open-pipe system, yet it has flows moving in two directions at the same time.

So it’s like a river going north and south at the same time. So when you say picture it, it’s actually one of the most beautiful things I’ve ever seen. And the biophysicists when they saw it for the first time, they said, “ This just can’t be true. How do they do it?”

**STROGATZ:**This is amazing. This is off topic, but I’m just gonna throw it out there but when I was a kid in high school, I had a science teacher who showed me how to do an experiment that Galileo had described in the 1600s, where Galileo said he took a little jug of water and another jug of wine, and then he could connect these two reservoirs, the wine on the bottom and the water on the top. And there’s this thin vertical tube connecting them. Galileo said that the wine will rise through the tube and the water will flow down through the tube, and they will pass through without mixing and they will trade places. And I actually did this experiment.

**KIERS:**Did it work?

**STROGATZ:**And it worked. They didn’t mix in the tube. My teacher took a photograph of it. It was published in a history of science magazine when I was 13 years old. The, the point being that a historian of science said Galileo was fudging and he had made up this experiment because we all know that when two things pass through the same tube, they would mix.

You’re telling me a story about two different flows through a whole network of tubes.

**KIERS:**Exactly, exactly.

**STROGATZ:**Am I on the right track thinking like this?

**KIERS:**You are kind of on the right track, and it’s something that is a big open question in our lab right now, so it’s something we’re constantly thinking about. I think I go to bed thinking about it and wake up thinking about it. But what you have to remember is that the diet that the plants give the fungi is full of fat, and fat doesn’t mix very well with water.

And so there are these things called condensates, which are these big lipid droplets inside the network. And what we think is happening is that there’s these beautiful molecular motors that are inside the network that actually drag the lipids, the fats, to the tip of the network so the fungus can use it to grow. And we think that’s what’s happening, is that when you pull these lipids on these… So a molecular motor, you can think of it as, a little railroad track that has, one of those cars on it that people move up and down and up and down to move forward. That’s what a, a molecular motor looks like.

**STROGATZ:**Uh-huh.

**KIERS:**And you can see this in the lab. It’s so beautiful to watch the lipids move inside on these tracks. But it’s not the only thing that’s happening, is that these, um, by the lipids in the molecular motors pulling the fluid, it actually creates a pressure. And so if you’re pulling one way and you’re- have a, an end that’s plugged up, it forces the liquid to go the other way because of pressure.

And so the fungus actually, we think, is opening and closing these beautiful aquaporins, these little pores that help regulate how much water is going in and out, and that’s helping drive pressure inside, in the network. And so it’s a combination of the active molecular motors pulling, but then these very fast flows that are created by the pressure inside the cell. And as a result, you get these very complex patterns inside. And because we can label the carbon, it’s this sort of beautiful fluorescent, almost looks like a lava lamp moving through a very thin liquid, a very thin tube, all the way up to the tip and back. And it’s mesmerizing.

**STROGATZ:**[_Laughs_] Well, I’m sure anyone listening to this can hear how excited you are by your own subject, and this is thrilling and infectious to listen to. But I wonder though if anyone is not getting it, can we just pan back in our story? Why should the average citizen care about these underground networks that they probably didn’t even know existed?

**KIERS:**Well, these networks, they really can support us in tackling some of the biggest challenges facing humanity today. I mean, they are incredibly important in regulating our climate. And that’s a really new field. So some work that we published in 2023 found that these mycorrhizal networks are processing about 13 billion tons of CO2 every year.

So that’s like roughly a third of emissions from fossil fuels. So to say that another way, plants are taking up all of this carbon from our atmosphere and then allocating about thirteen billion tons of that to networks every year. So they really help regulate our climate. And once that carbon is down in the soil, the networks bring it down deep where it can stay and not be released so much.

So, of course, the fungi are living, so they respire, so they lose some of that carbon, but they also create these very sticky, beautiful compounds that are very hard to break down, and so that helps keep carbon underground. You can think of them as like a scaffolding that sort of holds the soil together. If they weren’t there, the soil would just erode and disappear.

So, not only are they important in regulating our climate, but they also help with our ability to grow food. So, as I was saying, the plants really depend on these networks for their phosphorus uptake, for their nitrogen, for their water. Up to 80% of a plant’s phosphorus first passes through a fungal network. So, what that means is even the DNA, backbone, the phosphorus backbone of our own DNA first passed through a fungal network. Like we are made up of phosphorus that passed through fungi.

**STROGATZ:**Oh, that’s nice.

**KIERS:**It’s so beautiful. And they also, they really regulate water availability. New work has shown that they’re very good at breaking down pollutants and heavy metals. And so what we worry about is that people are not paying attention to these networks, and if we keep destroying them there’s chances for more increased global warming, accelerating biodiversity loss, and really disrupting the Earth’s nutrient cycles.

**STROGATZ:** Mmmm. Okay, very convincing answer. You’ve really made the case that we should care about them even though we may not be aware or able to see them.

**KIERS:**I think that’s the most important part is that people tend to assume that soils are sort of dead or inert. This is likely because, like, soil life has been largely invisible. And so a lot of what we do is trying to make that invisible life visible, and so that people actually start to see and connect with the underground, kind of flip their perspective and think about underground ecosystems as places where life begins.

**STROGATZ:**Let’s talk about that a little bit. I think that many of our listeners will already get this point, but I have to admit, it was relatively late in my life that I started to appreciate that dirt is not just dirt, that dirt is alive in all kinds of ways, and that by thinking about that, we can understand, like, why does a farmer rotate their crops or something like that. I mean, this isn’t exactly what we’re talking about here, but just help us understand what it means when someone says the soil is a living thing.

**KIERS:**So when we think about soils, one of the most surprising statistics that most people haven’t heard is that 59% of all species on Earth live underground. And so if even if we’re serious about just protecting biodiversity, this has to include life underground.

One of the problems I think, is just trying to make people curious, right? Trying to understand, so that they step on the Earth and they start thinking about all of the interactions that are happening right under their feet. I mean, without healthy soils, ecosystems collapse, lands degrade. There’s this beautiful balance of air and water and climate that really can’t be disrupted, and I think farmers are really good at knowing about that balance in many ways and trying to generate the soil, regenerate the soil, rather than just having it be something that’s constantly being extracted from.

**STROGATZ:**Mmm-hmmm. Okay, so let’s zoom in a little bit on some of the things that you already mentioned. I mean, you used the word symbiosis earlier, that the plants are providing carbon flows down to the fungi, the fungi are trading nitrogen and phosphorus back up. It all sounds like this is the language of markets and trading. It sounds like economics, and that’s one of the things that you’re known for is helping us see things through this market perspective.

So tell us about that. I mean, is it just like a cooperative market where there’s a division of labor — you do something I can’t do, so I do something you can’t do, and we’re both happy? Or is there any tension in this sort of system?

**KIERS:**These are all brilliant questions and ones that I’ve been asking myself for many decades now. And this idea of using an economic lens, it can really help us understand these trade dynamics. Now trade works because organisms, they all need slightly different resources, and access to those resources, they bring benefits. But also beyond co-dependence, I mean, there are bacterial organelles that have been synthesized into fungi. That seems like the boundary between separate organisms has also diffused, and that’s pretty remarkable. There also seems to be this kind of, like, evolutionary idea that pressure creates evolution. It drives evolution, right?

**STROGATZ:**Yeah, that’s right. We do use that phrase, right? Selective pressure. We tend to think, oh, stress is a bad thing. We need to reduce stress in our lives or conflict, and I think it’s an interesting instructive point that Toby makes that, yes, of course, you don’t wanna overdo it with stress and tension and all that, but a certain amount of tension or stress or competition can lead to complexity, she mentions, innovation. It does appear to be very deeply woven into the nature of life.

**LEVIN:**Yeah, I feel like there’s also a metaphor for life there somehow. You know, how to take lessons from nature and how to evolve.

**STROGATZ:**Anyway, we don’t have much choice. That does seem to be the way things are.

**LEVIN:**So these fungi are really so interconnected and so interdependent that, do they talk about that boundary of organisms where they have really begun to merge to some extent?

**STROGATZ:**Yeah, it’s very tricky to think about what’s an organism, what’s a system, an ecosystem, a population, a colony. It’s an issue we’ve gotten into with some of our other guests in _The Joy of Why._

It’s really maybe a case where our human-imposed distinctions may not line up very well with the way nature operates. We’re putting categories on things that are just more subtle than that.

**LEVIN:**I wonder if people are also thinking about ways to induce these networks to help clean up some of the climate crisis that we’re facing. If these are so influential and they have such an important role in terms of, if you like, the economics of the ecosystem or the economics of the biosphere, is there a way that we can guide a fungi to help clean up this mess?

**STROGATZ:**Hmm. You know, I don’t know that they need any encouragement from us. They just need protection to not have their ecosystems devastated. And, she did mention that a vast amount of these mycorrhizal networks are not the places being protected.

**LEVIN:**Wow, right.

**STROGATZ:**So, this is what she and her colleagues are trying to bring attention to. Because we don’t see them, we don’t notice or think about them but they may be just as important.

**LEVIN:**Yeah. Maybe nature will show us the way.

**STROGATZ:**Yeah. As always, it’s been a pleasure.

**LEVIN:**Thank you, Steve.

**STROGATZ:**See you next time.
