title: Probability Theory Pioneer Mark Kac on the Unpredictability of Creativity and the Two Types of Geniuses
content:
[![Image 1: Probability Theory Pioneer Mark Kac on the Unpredictability of Creativity and the Two Types of Geniuses](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/05/enigmasofchance.jpg?fit=320%2C489&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Enigmas-Chance-Autobiography-Alfred-Foundation/dp/0060154330/?tag=braipick-20)

The great Polish-American mathematician **Mark Kac** (August 3, 1914–October 26, 1984) possessed one of the most dazzling minds of the twentieth century. In pioneering probability theory, he paved the way for a radical new conception of truth and ushered in the first generation of scientists trained to think probabilistically — a more accurate assessment of knowledge, making room for uncertainty, be it scientific or otherwise. This probabilistic mode of judgment is all the more necessary today as the growing complexity of the world is swirling us into exponentially increasing uncertainty, which we attempt to tame through artificial absolutism.

Mathematics literally saved Kac’s life. His student work earned him a post-doctoral fellowship to study abroad, so he left Poland for Johns Hopkins University in December of 1938. World War II broke out months later. His entire family, along with millions of other Jews, was killed by the Nazis.

Kac went on to lead a long and creatively fertile life — one he considered, despite this unfathomable share of misfortune, a tremendously fortunate one. _“I must pay tribute to that powerful but capricious lady, Chance, who chose to bestow her beneficence on my personal life even though I spent much of my mathematical life trying to prove that she does not really exist,”_ he wrote with his characteristic mix of wit and wisdom in [**_Enigmas of Chance: An Autobiography_**](https://www.amazon.com/Enigmas-Chance-Autobiography-Alfred-Foundation/dp/0060154330/?tag=braipick-20) ([_public library_](http://www.worldcat.org/title/enigmas-of-chance-an-autobiography/oclc/11814594&referer=brief_results)) — a small, wonderful 1976 book I discovered via a passing mention in an [interview with the trailblazing astronomer Vera Rubin](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/04/18/vera-rubin-interview-women-in-science/). (Here is further proof of my longstanding conviction that [literature is the original Internet](https://onbeing.org/programs/maria-popova-cartographer-of-meaning-in-a-digital-age/) — such citations, allusions, and cross-references between books are the wondrous “hyperlinks” connecting human knowledge throughout our [“common record.”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2012/10/11/as-we-may-think-1945/))

[![Image 2: Mark Kac](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/05/markkac1.jpg?resize=680%2C993&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Enigmas-Chance-Autobiography-Alfred-Foundation/dp/0060154330/?tag=braipick-20)

Mark Kac

Kac writes:

> Creative people live in two worlds. One is the ordinary world which they share with others and in which they are not in any special way set apart from their fellow men. The other is private and it is in this world that the creative acts take place. It is a world with its own passions, elations and despairs, and it is here that, if one is as great as Einstein, one may even hear the voice of God. The two worlds are intimately and intricately connected. Jealousy, the desire for recognition and competitiveness, for example, are part of the ordinary world but they are among the forces which propel into the second. Similarly, dreams and triumphs in the second have a way of merging with less than lofty thoughts of rewards in the first.

With an eye to the particular challenge that autobiography presents to the creative person, he adds:

> To create a coherent and truthful picture of life in the two disparate and yet interrelated worlds is a nearly impossible task.

In discussing his great heroes and influences, Kac delineates another dichotomy in creative culture — the bifurcation of brilliance by degree and by kind:

> In science, as well as in other fields of human endeavor, there are two kinds of geniuses: the “ordinary” and the “magicians.” An ordinary genius is a [person] that you and I would be just as good as, if we were only many times better. There is no mystery as to how his mind works. Once we understand what he has done, we feel certain that we, too, could have done it. It is different with the magicians. They are, to use mathematical jargon, in the orthogonal complement of where we are and the working of their minds is for all intents and purposes incomprehensible. Even after we understand what they have done, the process by which they have done it is completely dark. They seldom, if ever, have students because they cannot be emulated and it must be terribly frustrating for a brilliant young mind to cope with the mysterious ways in which the magician’s mind works.

He points to the nuclear physicist Hans Bethe as an example of an “ordinary genius” and to [Richard Feynman](https://www.themarginalian.org/tag/richard-feynman/) as a “magician.” (Kac’s distinction appears in James Gleick’s [superb biography of Feynman](https://www.amazon.com/Genius-Life-Science-Richard-Feynman/dp/0679747044/?tag=braipick-20) and there is a high probability that it inspired the title of BBC’s documentary about the legendary physicist, [_No Ordinary Genius_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2011/12/14/bbcs-richard-feynman-no-ordinary-genius/).) I would add [Alan Turing](https://www.themarginalian.org/tag/alan-turing) to the “magicians” category, and of course [Albert Einstein](https://www.themarginalian.org/tag/albert-einstein/).

[![Image 3](https://i2.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/11/onabeamoflight5.jpg)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/12/30/on-a-beam-of-light-albert-einstein-radunsky/)

Illustration by Vladimir Radunsky for [_On a Beam of Light: A Story of Albert Einstein_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/12/30/on-a-beam-of-light-albert-einstein-radunsky/) by Jennifer Berne

In the postscript, Kac considers what lends mathematics its enduring enchantment — what renders people [besotted](http://www.onbeing.org/program/mathematics-purpose-and-truth/130) with it:

> Mathematics is an ancient discipline. For as long as we can reliably reach into the past, we can find its development intimately connected with the development of the whole of our civilization. For as long as we have a record of man’s curiosity and his quest for understanding, we find mathematics cultivated and cherished, practiced and taught. Throughout the ages it has stood as an ultimate in rational thought and as a monument to man’s desire to probe the workings of his own mind.
> 
> 
> […]
> 
> 
> The urge to understand and to create mathematics has always been remarkable, considering that those who have devoted their lives to the service of this aloof and elusive mistress could expect neither great material rewards nor widespread fame.

A champion of nuance, Kac challenges Bertrand Russell’s famous assertion that [“mathematics may be defined as the subject in which we never know what we are talking about, nor whether what we are saying is true.”](http://literaryjukebox.brainpickings.org/post/143798113017) Kac finds it to be a “dull and rather miserable picture of mathematics” and yet “not wholly wrong,” “just hopelessly incomplete and one-sided.” Instead, he considers what grants mathematics its richness as a mode of illuminating reality:

> I am reminded of something Balthazaar van der Pol, a great Dutch scientist and engineer who was also a fine musician, remarked to me about the music of Bach. “It is great,” he said, “because it is inevitable and yet surprising.” I have often thought about this lovely epigram in connection with mathematics… The inevitability is, in many cases, provided by logic alone, but the element of surprise must come from an insight outside the rigid confines of logic.

It warrants noting that the altogether marvelous [**_Enigmas of Chance_**](https://www.amazon.com/Enigmas-Chance-Autobiography-Alfred-Foundation/dp/0060154330/?tag=braipick-20) is part of a series of scientists’ autobiographies funded by the [Alfred P. Sloan Foundation](http://www.sloan.org/), which has probably done more for science and its social life than any other entity in the past half-century. Complement it with this [beautiful love letter to mathematics](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/02/22/james-joseph-sylvester-mathematics-address/) by the pioneering 19th-century English mathematician James Joseph Sylvester, the [illustrated life of the eccentric mathematical genius Paul Erdos](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/06/02/the-boy-who-loved-paul-erdos/), and the great English mathematician John Horton Conway on [tinkering, thinkering, and the art of being a professional nonunderstander](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/12/22/genius-at-play-siobhan-roberts/).

title: Nobel Laureate Doris Lessing on Breaking Free from the Prisons We Choose to Live Inside
content:
[![Image 1: Nobel Laureate Doris Lessing on Breaking Free from the Prisons We Choose to Live Inside](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/dorislessing_massey.jpg?fit=320%2C514&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Prisons-We-Choose-Live-Inside/dp/0060390778/?tag=braipick-20)

This is the history of the world: revolutionaries turning into tyrants, leaders who claim to stand with the masses turning the individuals within them on each other, stirring certainties and self-righteousness to distract from the uncomfortable unknowns, from the great open question of what makes us and keeps us human, and human together.

This is also the history of the world: artists — those [lighthouses of the spirit](https://www.themarginalian.org/2024/11/06/transition/) — speaking truth to power, placing imagination ahead of ideology, the soul above the self, [unselfing](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/10/21/iris-murdoch-unselfing/) us into seeing each other, into remembering, as James Baldwin told Margaret Mead in [their epochal conversation](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/03/19/a-rap-on-race-margaret-mead-and-james-baldwin/), that “we are still each other’s only hope.”

Born in Iran months after the end of the First World War and raised by farming parents in present-day Zimbabwe, **Doris Lessing** (October 22, 1919–November 17, 2013) was still a girl when she sensed something deeply wrong with the unquestioned colonial system of her world, with the oppression that was the axis of that world. By the time she was a young woman — a time when our urge to rebel against the broken system is fiery but we don’t yet have the tools to rebel intelligently, don’t yet know the right questions to ask in order to tell whether the answer we are holding up as an alternative is any better or worse — she rebelled by embracing Communism as “an interesting manifestation of popular will.” Working by that point as a telephone operator in England, she joined the Communist Party. “It was a conversion, apparently sudden, and total (though short-lived),” she would later recall. “Communism was in fact a germ or virus that had already been at work in me for a long time… because of my rejection of the repressive and unjust society of old white-dominated Africa.” It didn’t take her long to see the cracks in Communism. She left the party, discovered Sufism, grew fascinated with the nascent field of behavioral psychology and its revelatory, often disquieting findings about the inner workings of the mind, of its formidable powers to act and its immense vulnerabilities to being acted upon. But she found no ready-made answer to the problem of social harmony.

![Image 2](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/DorisLessing_TheMarginalian.jpg?resize=680%2C510&ssl=1)

And so, in that way artists have of complaining by creating, she devoted her life — almost a century of life, a century of world wars and violent uprisings, of changes unimaginable to her parents — to asking the difficult, clarifying questions that help us better understand what makes us human, how we allow ourselves to dehumanize others, and what it takes to cohere, as individuals and as societies. At 87, she became the oldest person to receive the Nobel Prize, awarded her for writing that “with scepticism, fire and visionary power has subjected a divided civilisation to scrutiny.”

In 1985, months after I was born under Bulgaria’s Communist dictatorship, Doris Lessing delivered Canada’s esteemed annual Massey Lectures, later adapted into a series of short essays under the haunting title [**_Prisons We Choose to Live Inside_**](https://www.amazon.com/Prisons-We-Choose-Live-Inside/dp/0060390778/?tag=braipick-20) ([_public library_](https://search.worldcat.org/title/74384615)) — a searching look at how it is that “we (the human race) are now in possession of a great deal of hard information about ourselves, but we do not use it to improve our institutions and therefore our lives,” lensed through a lucid faith that we have all the power, urgency, and dignity we need to choose otherwise, to use what we have learned about the worst of our nature to nurture and magnify the best of our nature, to figure out “how we behave so that we control the society and the society does not control us.”

[![Image 3](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/LittlePrince_Morgan-scaled.jpg?resize=680%2C453&ssl=1)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/02/03/exupery-little-prince-morgan-drawings/)

One of Antoine de Saint Exupéry’s [original watercolors for _The Little Prince_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/02/03/exupery-little-prince-morgan-drawings/). (Morgan Library & Museum)

In a sentiment Rebecca Solnit would echo three decades later in her modern classic [_Hope in the Dark_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/03/16/rebecca-solnit-hope-in-the-dark-2/), Lessing writes:

> This is a time when it is frightening to be alive, when it is hard to think of human beings as rational creatures. Everywhere we look we see brutality, stupidity, until it seems that there is nothing else to be seen but that — a descent into barbarism, everywhere, which we are unable to check. But I think that while it is true there is a general worsening, it is precisely because things are so frightening we become hypnotized, and do not notice — or if we notice, belittle — equally strong forces on the other side, the forces, in short, of reason, sanity and civilization.

To be realistic about our own nature, Lessing argues, requires attentiveness to both of these strands — the destructive and the creative. This is the cosmic mirror Maya Angelou held up to humanity in her [stunning space-bound poem](https://www.themarginalian.org/2018/05/09/a-brave-and-startling-truth-maya-angelou/), urging us to “learn that we are neither devils nor divines.” An epoch before her, Bertrand Russell — also a Nobel laureate in Literature, though trained as a scientist — [reckoned with our twin capacities](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/02/21/education-and-the-good-life-bertrand-russell/) to define them in elemental terms — “We construct when we increase the potential energy of the system in which we are interested, and we destroy when we diminish the potential energy.” — and in existential terms: “Construction and destruction alike satisfy the will to power, but construction is more difficult as a rule, and therefore gives more satisfaction to the person who can achieve it.”

Our sanity, Lessing observes, lies in “our capacity to be detached and unflattering about ourselves” — and in the understanding that our selves are not islanded in time but lineages of beliefs and tendencies with roots much longer than our lifetimes, not sovereign but contiguous with all the other selves that occupy the particular patch of spacetime we have been born into. It is vital, she insists, that we examine ourselves — our selves, and the constellation of selves that is our given society — from various elsewheres.

[![Image 4](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/Velocity_FelicitaSala.jpg)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2018/11/20/a-velocity-of-being-letters-to-a-young-reader/)

Art by Felicita Sala from [_A Velocity of Being: Letters to a Young Reader_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2018/11/20/a-velocity-of-being-letters-to-a-young-reader/).

This is why we need writers — those professional observers, in Susan Sontag’s [splendid definition](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/02/10/the-project-of-literature-susan-sontag-92y/), whose job it is to “pay attention to the world” and shine the light of that attention on every side of the kaleidoscope that is a given culture at a given time. A decade after Iris Murdoch wrote in her [superb reckoning with the role of literature in democracy](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/02/12/iris-murdoch-salvation-by-words/) that “tyrants always fear art because tyrants want to mystify while art tends to clarify,” Lessing writes:

> In totalitarian societies writers are distrusted for precisely this reason… Writers everywhere are aspects of each other, aspects of a function that has been evolved by society… Literature is one of the most useful ways we have of achieving this “other eye,” this detached manner of seeing ourselves; history is another.

Because we are the future of our own past, the posterity of our ancestors, looking back on history from our present vantage point offers fertile training ground for looking forward, for shaping the world of tomorrow. Lessing writes:

> Anyone who reads history at all knows that the passionate and powerful convictions of one century usually seem absurd, extraordinary, to the next. There is no epoch in history that seems to us as it must have to the people who lived through it. What we live through, in any age, is the effect on us of mass emotions and of social conditions from which it is almost impossible to detach ourselves.
> 
> 
> […]
> 
> 
> There is no such thing as my being in the right, my side being in the right, because within a generation or two, my present way of thinking is bound to be found perhaps faintly ludicrous, perhaps quite outmoded by new development — at the best, something that has been changed, all passion spent, into a small part of a great process, a development.

![Image 5](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/DorisLessing_NPG_TheMarginalian1.jpg?resize=680%2C685&ssl=1)

Doris Lessing, 1950s. (National Portrait Gallery, London)

In consonance with Carl Sagan’s admonition against [“the sense that we have a monopoly on the truth”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/11/09/carl-sagan-demon-haunted-world-ignorance-compassion/) and with Joan Didion’s admonition against [mistaking self-righteousness for morality](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/12/05/joan-didion-on-morality/), Lessing offers:

> This business of seeing ourselves as in the right, others in the wrong; our cause as right, theirs as wrong; our ideas as correct, theirs as nonsense, if not as downright evil… Well, in our sober moments, our human moments, the times when we think, reflect, and allow our rational minds to dominate us, we all of us suspect that this “I am right, you are wrong” is, quite simply, nonsense. All history, development goes on through interaction and mutual influence, and even the most violent extremes of thought, of behaviour, become woven into the general texture of human life, as one strand of it. This process can be seen over and over again in history. In fact, it is as if what is real in human development — the main current of social evolution — cannot tolerate extremes, so it seeks to expel extremes and extremists, or to get rid of them by absorbing them into the general stream.

Looking back on the colonialist Zimbabwe of her childhood, on the “prejudiced, ugly, ignorant” attitudes of the ruling whites, she reflects:

> These attitudes were assumed to be unchallengeable and unalterable, though the merest glance at history would have told them (and many of them were educated people) that it was inevitable their rule would pass, that their certitudes were temporary.

At the center of Lessing’s inquiry is the paradox of how seemingly sound-minded, kind-hearted people get enlisted in ideologies of oppression. Kierkegaard [had written](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/11/26/kierkegaard-individual-crowd-conformity-minority/) in the Golden Age of European revolutions — those idealistic but imperfect attempts to unify fractured feudal duchies into free nations, attempts that modeled the possibility of a United States of America — that “the evolution of the world tends to show the absolute importance of the category of the individual apart from the crowd,” that “truth always rests with the minority, and the minority is always stronger than the majority, because… the strength of a majority is illusory, formed by the gangs who have no opinion.” An epoch and a world order later, Lessing considers how regimes of terror take hold:

> Nearly everyone in such situations behaves automatically. But there is always the minority who do not, and it seems to me that our future, the future of everybody, depends on this minority. And that we should be thinking of ways to educate our children to strengthen this minority and not, as we mostly do now, to revere the pack.

[![Image 6](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/bearisneveralone1.jpg)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2023/11/26/bear-is-never-alone/)

Art by Jeska Verstegen from [_Bear Is Never Alone_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2023/11/26/bear-is-never-alone/) by Marc Veerkamp

The mess we have made, she intimates, may be the most effective teaching tool we have — a living admonition against doing the same, a clarion call to rebel by doing otherwise:

> Perhaps it is not too much to say that in these violent times the kindest, wisest wish we have for the young must be: “We hope that your period of immersion in group lunacy, group self-righteousness, will not coincide with some period of your country’s history when you can put your murderous and stupid ideas into practice. “If you are lucky, you will emerge much enlarged by your experience of what you are capable of in the way of bigotry and intolerance. You will understand absolutely how sane people, in periods of public insanity, can murder, destroy, lie, swear black is white.”

As for us, here in the roiling mess, our sole salvation lies in learning to “live our lives with minds free of violent and passionate commitment, but in a condition of intelligent doubt about ourselves and our lives, a state of quiet, tentative, dispassionate curiosity.” Lessing writes:

> While all these boilings and upheavals go on, at the same time, parallel, continues this other revolution: the quiet revolution, based on sober and accurate observation of ourselves, our behaviour, our capacities… If we decided to use it, [we may] transform the world we live in. But it means making that deliberate step into objectivity and away from wild emotionalism, deliberately choosing to see ourselves as, perhaps, a visitor from another planet might see us.

[![Image 7](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/kamauandzuzu4.jpg)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2024/08/30/kamau-zuzu-find-a-way/)

Art by Diana Ejaita from [_Kamau & ZuZu Find a Way_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2024/08/30/kamau-zuzu-find-a-way/) by poet Aracelis Girmay

This, in fact, was the conditional clause in Baldwin’s words to Mead — in order to be “each other’s only hope,” [he said](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/03/19/a-rap-on-race-margaret-mead-and-james-baldwin/), we ought to be “as clear-headed about human beings as possible.” This, too, was Maya Angelou’s conditional optimism for humanity: “That is when, and only when, we come to it” — to that [“Brave and Startling Truth,”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2018/05/09/a-brave-and-startling-truth-maya-angelou/) balanced on the fulcrum of our conflicted capacities, “that we are the possible, we are the miraculous, the true wonder of this world.”

title: What We Can Save In A Time Of Endings
content:
Credits

Kat Hill is a writer and researcher based in Scotland. Her forthcoming book is “Endlings: A Journey into the Last of Things.” She has held fellowships and positions at numerous academic institutions including the Institute for Advanced Study and Oxford University. She is currently the creative director of Upland Arts Development in Scotland.

_Nicholas J.R. White is a photographer living on the Isle of Skye. He is a recipient of the Royal Photographic Society Environmental Bursary and is the 2026 Ampersand Foundation/Photoworks Fellow._

HAPPISBURGH, England —Off the coast of Norfolk on edge of the North Sea, the ocean can seem calm, but the waters are deceptive. Beneath the marbled brown lie sand banks and submerged mountains waiting to ensnare unsuspecting ships. Happisburgh (pronounced Hays-burro) is a small, pretty town, its narrow roads lined by houses with walls made of flint pressed into mortar. The beach roads all have names like Stone’s Throw or Cliff Top, and the sea has always been present in people’s lives. But inching ever closer for years, now its incursions are rapid and frightening.

The light changed suddenly. Over my shoulder the sky was dark with rain that towered in hazy columns against a thunderous glow. It rolled over the beach, over the houses, falling into the sea, billowing over the crumbling cliff edge. Lightning split the blackness and the clouds rumbled. Gulls soared like scraps of loose paper and sand martins wheeled in a frenzy, seeking refuge. For a moment, the world had ended. Then it was clear again: sun shining, birds calling, people laughing.

I was looking out to submerged places, out to the infamous Doggerland. Places with names and identities that no longer exist here. Not in the way they used to. Under the water, now lost to the waves, they live on in their cartographic afterlife. Eccles-on-Sea is named after a church, but the original place of worship is long gone, and the collection of bungalows that form the village hunker behind protecting dunes and a sea wall. This is the Bush Estate, a so-called Plotland community, the name given to settlements that emerged during an early 20th century movement of working-class people buying cheap land on the seaside. Most of the houses, along with St. Mary’s church, were washed away in the 17th century; for a time, only the tower remained, the sea creeping closer and sand drifting over the stones at its base. For years, it acted as a sailor’s beacon until it too succumbed to the waves. Now only a fragment of the bottom wall apparently remains visible at a low spring tide, though I did not see it. Dunwich, a thriving port town just to the south along the coast, was swept to sea centuries earlier.

They remain a warning to us all of what may befall a place, consigned to ruin, memory and legend.

We live at a time when endings are all around us. But endings are never straightforward. An ending may be made up of many moments. Sometimes, we don’t know when things have truly receded from our world, and it can be difficult to determine what to care about, how and when. Questions about what to save become terribly real.

Standing on the Norfolk coast, I thought how odd it was to both observe an ending and to be caught up in it. In one sense the decline is apparent and unavoidable: Cliffs have crumbled, houses are gone, the end has happened. But in another, it’s an ending in a constant process of becoming, never starting or finishing, always ongoing. Such a loss carries emotional and philosophical weight across time, where salvation and survival ebb and flow.

The communities here seemed to be in the middle of a slow war, waiting for an enemy who would inevitably arrive no matter what watch they keep. It was an apocalyptic feeling: dark skies, rock defenses, the bones of former homes, tumbledown walls and shattered fences. And yet, the apocalypse seemed simultaneously distant, like a thing of fable, impossible to actually happen.

Writing after World War I, after the destruction wrought on the confidence of Europe, essayist Paul Valéry reflected: “W⁠e had long heard tell of whole worlds that had vanished, of empires sunk without a trace. … But the disasters that had sent them down were, after all, none of our affair. Elam, Nineveh, Babylon were but beautiful vague names.” Yet then he too felt that same fear of collapse after witnessing the horror of war and the devastated world that came after. “We are aware now that a civilisation has the same fragility as a life.” Worlds can end. Choose to look and absence and scars tell stories.

> “No one wants to be made to give something up or be told it’s time to surrender.”

“How can we learn to die?” the philosophers Fernando Flores and B. Scot Rousse asked. But confronting us today is not just individual death, nor even the prospect of human extinction, but the possibility of the disappearance of all our ways of life and being. This is what Jonathan Lear called ontological vulnerability, the sense that a world of meaning might collapse. His book “Radical Hope” was focused on the Crow people of the American West and referred to an “uncanny sense of menace … a shared vulnerability that we cannot quite name.” As Plenty Coups, the last great chief of the Crow, said shortly before he died in 1932: “When the buffalo went away the hearts of my people fell to the ground, and they could not lift them up again. After this nothing happened.”

On the Norfolk coast, the pub, the church, the road and the shop might all soon be gone. Maybe the homes will remain, maybe not. Climate change may not kill everyone, but it may destroy the things that give life meaning. It’s one thing to survive, another to live. When you know that the flood will rush in, the fire will burn, the end is coming, what would you do? And what would you save? One option is to improve defenses: shelter cities and rebuff the rising tide from California to Yorkshire to Pacific islands. Another solution is to move.

In the U.K., the Shoreline Management Plans (SMPs), a series of complex strategic outlines, determine the futures of coastal regions, weighing up priority places to spend money and build walls. They read like military plans. The options are do nothing, maintain defenses, extend defenses or realign coastal assets. Hold the line. Fortify. Resist. Retreat.

In some instances, we have no choice but to protect something because it would do too much damage to leave it undefended. There are nuclear power plants in vulnerable places along the U.K. coast. Sizewell B in Suffolk had been slated to be decommissioned by 2035 but was recently given a new lease of life until 2055; Sizewell C, is newly under construction and due to be operational in the 2030s. It has an elaborate defense plan: raised up on a 7-meter (23-foot) platform with walls. Some say it’s not high enough. Modeling of sea level rise goes to 2140 and doesn’t take into account the long future of nuclear waste. Moreover, walls and floodgates were designed for receding high waters, not permanent rise. They endanger places nearby by preventing the natural movement of sand.

Sellafield, on the Cumbrian Coast, is the most dangerous nuclear site in Europe. It’s always present, the golf ball dome and the chimneys looming in the distance, a crumbling facade behind the farm shops and fells of the Lake District. At night the lights glow with an ominous red haze. It is a hazardous place. High-level waste is stored in legacy silos and ponds. The Magnox Swarf Silo is just leaking into the ground.⁠ Just down the road, with armored fences on the edge of people’s homes, is the LLW Repository, the dumping ground for all low-level nuclear waste in the U.K. Long-term, the authorities aim to bury all this in the sea, deep down in a Geological Disposal Facility. But for now, they shore them up against the rising sea because to do otherwise would risk it all leaching out in catastrophic fashion. Toxic waste that never becomes safe and cannot be moved will have to be fortified.

The houses on Braystones Beach below Sellafield will not be afforded the same protection. Once, they were railway carriages that brought and housed the workers to build the line along the coast; now, some have been developed into dwellings. Like the Plotland homes of Norfolk, they are marginal communities, places pushed to the edge. Winter high tides have a 7-meter (23-foot) range, with storms whipping up surging waves, ⁠and the row of single-story dwellings will often have the sea lapping at their doors; rocks and buoys, dredged up and dragged into shore, crash against homes. The inhabitants are determined to stay: They like living here in the wildness and wind. It’s part of the attraction, one woman told me, but they have resorted to building their own walls by claiming boulders and piling gravel and stones into embankments in front of their homes. I stood on the hill above and the small low-slung huts looked like a wall surrounding a fortress, a kind of defense protecting the aging nuclear plant. The Cumbria Coastal Strategy is dismissive of the value of the huts: “The majority of the frontage is undefended and there is no economic justification to providing significant investment at the present time.”

Famously, in 2019, the media condemned a seaside village in Wales called Fairbourne to be abandoned to the sea. House prices plummeted overnight, investment trickled away and the residents were labeled as Britain’s first climate refugees. Locals mobilized against the process of “managed retreat,” but the reputational damage was done and trust was destroyed. Insurance policies, which after all are a bet on the future, often will no longer cover homes in these coastal places.

> “Choose to look and absence and scars tell stories.”

There are already ruins and remnants aplenty on the Norfolk coast. It’s littered with the remains of Norman castles and military lookouts. Of all the things we could protect, is it worth saving ruins? Should we simply let them be committed to the memory of the sea? They are more than crumbling walls or upturned pillboxes — they are reminders of our past, anchors that root us to a sense of history and landscape. Just like with everything else, there’ll only be certain ruins designated as important and worth protecting. This is true of any heritage site, not just those threatened by climate change. As Gavin Lucas writes, “entropy is a social as well as a natural phenomenon.”

A recent National Trust report admitted it could not contain threats to coastal sites and aims to work “with the grain of nature.” On the coast of Caithness in Scotland’s far northeast, there are castles at every bay and promontory exposed to the ravages of the sea. One, Castle Sinclair Girnigoe, an impressive northern fortress, was listed on the World Monument Fund’s Monuments Watch in 2002. The complex of structures, dating back to the 15th century and once owned by Clan Sinclair, has received funds to stabilize and conserve the structure. Just along the coast, however, is Castle Bucholie, listed by Historic Environment Scotland, but without the same resources to protect it from its fate.

“Old” ruins were once homes or lives. The world is ephemeral. Preservation suggests we can protect things in the future by putting them on lists, but that’s not really true. The Caithness castles lean into the sea, and the empty windows look out to the water like screaming faces. Girnigoe Sinclair reopened with much fanfare in 2010, but the slow creep of time continues regardless of how much attention is given to it. Transience may be an opportunity to tell complex stories though; “managed ruination” can be a way to write what the cultural geographer Caitlin DeSilvey refers to as an “anticipatory history” of absence.

When I visited, Castle Sinclair’s wooden drawbridge was closed and the walls were covered in scaffolding. It is being reclaimed not just by the sea but by nature. Nesting fulmars stared from a window, and marsh orchids were growing out of the turf that covered the ruined walls.

Sea level rise and climate change threaten the nonhuman world, too. I saw ringed plovers on the beach near Sellafield, sand martins on the crumbling cliffs of the Norfolk coast. Signs warn people away from their nesting sites.

Norfolk’s water systems — the great expanses of the Broads, mudflats and marshes — are increasingly susceptible to the incursion of salty waves. The complex estuarine networks are like arteries that get pumped full of seawater when storm surges come. Salty waters kill invertebrates on which nesting waders feed, and wash away habitat.

Nonhuman environments are being squeezed, but who wants to save the sand martins or the butterflies when homes and businesses are at risk? Something must be sacrificed, and “sacrifice zone” is a term becoming increasingly common in discussions about environmental justice. It’s a word in the language of sanctity, martyrdom and faith — an act of giving something up to a higher purpose, to a god or to a devil. It asks that we think about death as something. It asks that we consider who to make a victim. If we build sea walls, we destroy marshland. If we protect nuclear waste, we condemn coastal communities.

No one wants to be made to give something up or be told it’s time to surrender. As I talked to people in Norfolk, Cumbria and Scotland, the rising sea was ever present in their minds, yet they were also persistent and stubborn. This was their home. What else were they supposed to do?

Part of the problem is that ends are not neat, and these are really debates about when an ending is inevitable, when it is declared and who gets to declare it. Sometimes the world may come and go in an instant but more often there is a slow disintegration of crumbling and drifting. Despite it all, it’s not easy to leave the thing that gives your world meaning and stability.

On a beach railing I found on the coast of Norfolk, there’s a sticker of a man. Rocks and flowers are arranged around the picture, with words of affectionate remembrance. Nearby is a bench with an inscription to a young biker who loved the view of the sea. The bench and the flowers will be gone soon, such small but momentous reminders of the persistence of love and memory in absence. Is this the time, when past and memory are done, when “nothing happens”?

> “Sometimes the world may come and go in an instant but more often there is a slow disintegration of crumbling and drifting.”

Because that’s the thing about these decisions. They are not just cold calculations, but about love, even when an end comes. The residents in Happisburgh and nearby Mundesley are worried about the churches that are threatened by the sea, which will undermine the graves of their family members and community. At St. Mary’s in Happisburgh, there’s a mass grave for sailors who drowned in the deep. Their bones are now being returned to the sea, and with them the memory of their lives.

I wandered into the church and saw a woman tending to the flowers on the altar, a wheelbarrow full of blooms next to her. In a pew, a man sat watching her as the sun streamed in through the glass, illuminating the dancing dust. Richard and Joan have lived and worked here all their lives, both baptized in the centuries-old font.

“One day the sea will take it.” That’s what she says. She knows this is true but she tends the church anyway because it is part of her past. It dates to the 14th century; its peal of eight bells ring every Wednesday. There are legends around here that you can hear the drowned bells of Dunwich or Eccles-on-Sea. I’ve heard a similar tale of the mythical city of Ys, submerged beneath the waves, whose cathedral bell still rings.

There’s another bell on the beach at Happisburgh, designed by artist Marcus Vergette, that rings with the tide. Vergette told me that the bell was the perfect design for the sea. Bells disrupt space. They have a history and personality; they have names. Bells rang for death and life, funeral and marriage, celebration, announcement, mourning or warning. They communicate the passing of time and the ritual of life, and a bell’s back and forthness expresses the liminality of the coast. It is, he said, a particularly suitable form for the shifting sands of life, and to express the ambiguity of loss and desire.

I stood on the beach and listened to it. It tolled for time, for tide, for life and death. It was a liturgy of loss, but it was also a celebration and a call to joy and worship, perhaps even hope or the new dawn of a day.

What hope could it ring for? Lear believed in the vulnerability of our world but also a kind of radical hope even in absence and loss. Perhaps those places that are gone could have an afterlife. Recently archaeologists recorded oral histories around Happisburgh and scanned and 3D-photographed the church so it can live on in some form. Whole countries are adopting this approach. Tuvalu, a Pacific Island nation comprising small islets and low-lying atolls, is aiming to become the first “digital nation.” Seen from the air it is a ring of land in a backdrop of blue, a thin coral halo sinking rapidly. Tuvalu will not accept its fate as a victim; it will not just give into the inevitable end handed to it by the global forces of destruction.

Radical hope is possible, Lear writes, because we can have courage. Courage is an important virtue because it recognizes that we are “finite erotic creatures. … As finite creatures we are vulnerable: we may suffer physical and emotional injury, we may make significant mistakes, even the concepts with which we understand ourselves and the world may collapse — and yet as erotic creatures we reach out to the world and try to embrace it.”

I caught the last light of the day at the church in Mundesley. The golden sun escaped from underneath the granite clouds and it washed the world gold. Just for a moment. A great rainbow arced overhead, a sign of hope and peace after the storm, the color that returned after the biblical flood.

There may not be a world of pure hope for these coastal villages, because there will be losses. Even with an ending, we can consider what practices of courage, care and value to adopt, and what can be salvaged as we build defenses, remember and protect elsewhere. The economy of salvation is never straightforward, so reach out and embrace the world even as it disappears.
